title: Patrick's Confession
hookLine: Patrick's own words begin: I, Patrick, a sinner

lines: A SHORT BOOK IN ROUGH LATIN.
cards: Ego Patricius peccator rusticissimus. I, Patrick, a sinner, very unlearned. Those are the first words of a short document in rough Latin, written by the man himself, in what he calls his old age.
It doesn't begin with a miracle, or a boast, or a list of churches founded. It's a man telling the truth about himself, and giving thanks. He called it his confession.

teach.h: A DEACON'S SON WHO DIDN'T KNOW GOD.
teach.b: First, where he starts. Patrick names his father, a deacon, and his grandfather, a priest. He grew up in a Christian family in Britain, and then, he says plainly, he didn't know God.
Raiders seized him from his father's estate and carried him off to Ireland, a captive. He doesn't dress it up. He says he deserved to be taken, because he and the others had turned away from God.
Second, captivity. He was put to tending flocks, out in the cold, the snow, the rain. And there, he says, the love of God grew in him.
He prayed many times in the day and again in the night. The place of his slavery became the place he met God. Third, the voice.
One night he heard in his sleep that his ship was ready. He ran, crossed a long distance, found a ship, and after hardships came home. A few years later, back with his family, he had a dream.
A man came from Ireland carrying letters, and Patrick read the heading of one: the voice of the Irish. He heard them calling him to come and walk among them again.

teach.h: A SLAVE IN THE FIELDS, PRAYING.
teach.b: He went back, to the land where he'd been a slave.
Fourth, why it opens with sinner.
Patrick wrote the confession, he says, to give thanks, and to answer people who doubted him.
He's embarrassed by his Latin, and says so more than once. He doesn't make himself the hero. In his telling, the story belongs to God, who found a boy in a field.

how: Catholics keep Saint Patrick's feast day, and some read his Confession, or the prayer known as his Breastplate, which tradition attributes to him, on that day.

s: Patrick's Confession tells how he drove out the snakes
there are no snakes in it, and no shamrock. it's his own account of captivity, prayer and return.
Patrick says he didn't know God as a boy
he grew up in a Christian family, and says plainly he didn't know God.
Patrick boasts of his fine Latin
he calls himself very unlearned, and is embarrassed by his Latin.

games.q: you're Patrick, home again after escaping slavery. in a dream, the voice of the Irish calls you back. what do you do?
o: stay home; you've suffered enough there.
go back, to the land where you were a slave.
send someone else in your place.
games.why: he went back to Ireland. the place of his captivity became the place of his life's work.

practice: Patrick started with his name and the plain truth, so try the same, on paper or in your head: your first name, and one true thing you'd usually leave out of the story.
Not a punishment, not a speech, just honest: I, Sam, have been short with people I love this week, or I, Ana, am more scared than I let on.
Read it back once without arguing with it, and if you pray, hand it to God the way Patrick handed over his.
